qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: A monument at Saratoga National Historical Park honors this man’s wounded leg with a carved boot but leaves out his name. He was shot in that leg, which had also been wounded at Quebec in 1775, while attacking a redoubt held by German troops in October 1777.
tossups.r: Earlier, he had helped Ethan Allen capture Fort Ticonderoga. For 10 points, name this American general who later tried to hand West Point to the British.

tossups.p: At the U.S. Military Academy, a plaque honoring this general in the Old Cadet Chapel shows only his rank and a birth year, not his name. In 1780, this man wrote a pass for a British officer who was traveling under the name “John Anderson.”
tossups.r: That officer, John André [“AHN-dray”], was caught carrying plans of West Point. For 10 points, name this American general who turned traitor.

tossups.p: In October 1776, this man’s small fleet of hastily built gunboats and galleys fought a much stronger British fleet near Valcour Island on Lake Champlain. Although he lost most of his ships, the fight delayed a British invasion from Canada until the next year.
tossups.r: Four years later, he plotted to surrender West Point. For 10 points, name this general who became America’s most famous traitor.

tossups.p: In the fall of 1775, this man led more than a thousand soldiers up the Kennebec River through the Maine wilderness, where cold and hunger forced many to turn back. On the last day of that year, he and Richard Montgomery attacked Quebec City in a snowstorm, and he was wounded in the leg.
tossups.r: Montgomery was killed in the failed attack. For 10 points, name this general who later plotted to give West Point to the British.

tossups.p: This officer held a commission from Massachusetts but had to share command with Ethan Allen and the Green Mountain Boys when they captured Fort Ticonderoga [“ty-kon-der-OH-guh”] in May 1775. Days later, he sailed north on Lake Champlain and raided Fort St. Johns in Canada.
tossups.r: Henry Knox later hauled that fort’s cannons to Boston. For 10 points, name this patriot who later became a traitor by plotting to surrender West Point.

tossups.p: While serving as military commander of Philadelphia, this man married Peggy Shippen, a young woman from a wealthy family who had been friendly with British officers during the city’s occupation. Pennsylvania officials accused him of misusing his post, and his court-martial ended with a reprimand from George Washington.
tossups.r: Peggy later helped him plot treason. For 10 points, name this general who tried to surrender West Point to the British in 1780.

tossups.p: In secret letters, this man used the code name “Gustavus,” while his British contact signed as “John Anderson.” When he learned that his contact had been captured near Tarrytown, this man fled from his headquarters and escaped down the Hudson River to the British warship _Vulture_.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this general whose plot to hand West Point to the British fell apart in 1780.

tossups.p: As a brigadier general in the British army, this man led a raid on Richmond, Virginia, in January 1781. Later that year, he led an attack on New London, Connecticut, not far from his hometown of Norwich, and much of New London was burned.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this former American general who had switched sides after his plot to surrender West Point failed.

tossups.p: Congress angered this man in 1777 by promoting five officers with less seniority over him. After his horse was shot out from under him at the Battle of Ridgefield, Connecticut, he was finally made a major general, but at first Congress did not give back his seniority.
tossups.r: Such slights helped push him toward treason. For 10 points, name this general who plotted to give West Point to the British.

tossups.p: Three militiamen, including John Paulding, stopped a traveler near Tarrytown, New York, and found papers hidden in his stocking that described the defenses of a fort this man commanded. That traveler was tried and executed as a spy at Tappan in October 1780.
tossups.r: The fort was West Point. For 10 points, name this American general whose plot was exposed when John André was captured.

tossups.p: After the Battle of Freeman’s Farm, this general argued so bitterly with his commander that he was relieved of his duties, though he stayed in camp. Weeks later, he rode into the fighting anyway and rallied American troops at Bemis Heights, where Daniel Morgan’s riflemen also fought.
tossups.r: His commander was Horatio Gates. For 10 points, name this hero of the Saratoga campaign who later turned traitor.

tossups.p: In August 1777, this general helped end the British siege of Fort Stanwix in New York by sending a captured Loyalist to spread rumors that a huge American army was coming. Barry St. Leger’s Native allies left, and St. Leger retreated.
tossups.r: Weeks later, he was wounded at Saratoga. For 10 points, name this American general who later betrayed his country at West Point.

tossups.p: When George Washington arrived at this man’s headquarters in September 1780, this man’s wife acted so upset and confused that Washington and Alexander Hamilton believed she knew nothing of her husband’s plans. Historians later found that she had helped pass his secret messages.
tossups.r: She was Peggy Shippen. For 10 points, name this American general who had just fled after trying to betray West Point.

tossups.p: Before the Revolution, this man ran an apothecary shop and bookstore in New Haven and sailed his own trading ships to the West Indies and Canada. When news of Lexington and Concord arrived in 1775, he led his militia company to demand the keys to New Haven’s powder house.
tossups.r: He later plotted to hand West Point to the British. For 10 points, name this Connecticut patriot who became a traitor.

tossups.p: After the Revolution, this man lived for several years as a merchant in Saint John, New Brunswick, before settling in London, where he died in 1801. The British had paid him and made him a brigadier general for switching sides, but many British officers refused to trust him.
tossups.r: He had plotted to surrender West Point. For 10 points, name this American general whose name became another word for “traitor.”

clues.t: Plotted in 1780 to hand the American fort at West Point, New York, over to the British
His name became another word for “traitor”; he escaped and joined the British army
His British contact, Major John André, was caught with the fort’s plans and executed as a spy
A hero of the Saratoga campaign (1777), where he was shot in the leg
Captured Fort Ticonderoga with Ethan Allen and the Green Mountain Boys (May 1775)
Led a march through the Maine wilderness and attacked Quebec with Richard Montgomery (1775); wounded in the leg
His makeshift fleet fought the Battle of Valcour Island on Lake Champlain (1776), delaying a British invasion
Quarreled with Horatio Gates, who took away his command, but fought anyway at Bemis Heights
Married Peggy Shippen of Philadelphia, who helped him plot treason
Military commander of Philadelphia (1778); his court-martial ended with a reprimand from Washington
As a British brigadier general, raided Richmond, Virginia, and New London, Connecticut (1781)
Bitter after Congress promoted five officers with less seniority over him (1777); also deep in debt
Saratoga’s Boot Monument honors his wounded leg without naming him
His plaque in West Point’s Old Cadet Chapel shows only his rank and a birth year, not his name
Wrote secret letters under the code name “Gustavus”; André used the name “John Anderson”
Escaped down the Hudson River to the British warship _Vulture_
André was caught near Tarrytown by three militiamen, including John Paulding, with papers in his stocking; executed at Tappan
His horse was shot from under him at the Battle of Ridgefield, Connecticut (1777); then made a major general
Helped end Barry St. Leger’s siege of Fort Stanwix (1777) by having a captured Loyalist spread rumors of a huge army
His wife convinced Washington and Alexander Hamilton that she knew nothing of the plot
Ran an apothecary shop and bookstore in New Haven; demanded the keys to the town’s powder house (1775)
Lived as a merchant in Saint John, New Brunswick, then died in London (1801)
Held a Massachusetts commission at Ticonderoga, so he argued with Ethan Allen over who was in charge; then raided Fort St. Johns
Marched up the Kennebec River to Quebec; Daniel Morgan fought beside him at Quebec and at Saratoga

trap.title: Hero first, traitor later
trap.body: Early clues describe Benedict Arnold as an American hero, so players often buzz with a different patriot named in the question: Ethan Allen (Fort Ticonderoga), Horatio Gates (who got the credit for Saratoga), Daniel Morgan, or Richard Montgomery. Late clues about the West Point plot tempt players to say John André, the British officer who was caught, instead of the American general who plotted.
trap.fix: Arnold clues: a leg wounded at both Quebec and Saratoga, the fleet at Valcour Island, the quarrel with Gates, Peggy Shippen, the code name “Gustavus,” and the _Vulture_. If the question asks for “this British officer” or “this spy,” say André; “this American general” means Arnold.

topics.name: Boston
topics.kicker: Capital of Massachusetts · Cradle of the American Revolution
topics.briefing: Boston was founded in 1630 by Puritans led by John Winthrop, who hoped their colony would be “a city upon a hill” for the whole world to watch. More than a century later, its streets and harbor saw the Boston Massacre, the Boston Tea Party, and the start of Paul Revere’s midnight ride. Visitors can walk the 2.5-mile Freedom Trail past its historic sites, and the city claims American firsts like the oldest public park and the first subway.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This city was named for a port town in Lincolnshire, England, where the Puritan minister John Cotton preached before he sailed to New England in 1633. Its settlers first called its hilly peninsula Trimountaine, and the Native name for that peninsula was Shawmut.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this city founded by John Winthrop’s Puritans in 1630, the capital of Massachusetts.

tossups.p: William Blaxton, an English clergyman who already lived alone on this city’s peninsula, invited a group of Puritans to move there from Charlestown because it had fresh springs of water. The leader of those Puritans had preached that their colony would be “as a city upon a hill.”
tossups.r: That leader was John Winthrop. For 10 points, name this city founded in 1630, which became the capital of Massachusetts.

tossups.p: During a 1721 smallpox epidemic in this city, Cotton Mather urged people to try inoculation, a practice he had learned about from an enslaved African man named Onesimus. Doctor Zabdiel Boylston then inoculated his own young son and more than two hundred other people.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New England city, where Puritans led by John Winthrop had settled in 1630.

tossups.p: In 1846, William Morton gave the first public demonstration of ether as a surgical anesthetic in this city, in an operating room later nicknamed the Ether Dome. Thirty years later, Alexander Graham Bell made the first telephone call here, calling out to his assistant, Thomas Watson.
tossups.r: Both happened in the city where Paul Revere began his midnight ride. For 10 points, name this capital of Massachusetts.

tossups.p: Governor Calvin Coolidge became nationally famous in 1919 when he declared that there is “no right to strike against the public safety” during a walkout by this city’s police. Earlier that year, a giant tank burst in this city’s North End, flooding the streets with molasses and killing 21 people.
tossups.r: Both events happened in the city where the Sons of Liberty dumped tea into the harbor in 1773. For 10 points, name this Massachusetts capital.

tossups.p: Patriots met so often in this city’s Faneuil [“FAN-yul”] Hall, a marketplace and meeting hall donated by a merchant, that it was nicknamed the “Cradle of Liberty.” In July 1776, the Declaration of Independence was read aloud from the balcony of this city’s Old State House.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this city where Samuel Adams and the Sons of Liberty organized protests against British taxes.

tossups.p: Parliament’s Port Act closed this city’s harbor in 1774 until the East India Company was repaid for property destroyed there, and General Thomas Gage arrived to govern the colony. Other colonies sent food and supplies to help its people.
tossups.r: The destroyed property was 342 chests of tea. For 10 points, name this city where the Sons of Liberty held a famous Tea Party in 1773.

tossups.p: Every March 17, this city’s county celebrates Evacuation Day, marking the day in 1776 when General William Howe’s British army sailed away. Howe left after George Washington placed cannons hauled from Fort Ticonderoga by Henry Knox on Dorchester Heights, overlooking the harbor.
tossups.r: The Battle of Bunker Hill had been fought nearby the year before. For 10 points, name this Massachusetts city that British troops had first occupied in 1768.

tossups.p: Sexton Robert Newman hung two lanterns in the steeple of a church in this city to signal that British troops were crossing the water by boat. That signal was arranged by a silversmith from this city, who then rode to Lexington to warn Samuel Adams and John Hancock.
tossups.r: That silversmith, Paul Revere, also made a famous engraving of a 1770 massacre in this city. For 10 points, name this capital of Massachusetts.

tossups.p: Augustus Saint-Gaudens made a bronze memorial on this city’s Common to Robert Gould Shaw and the Black regiment he led in the Civil War, the unit shown in the film _Glory_. Decades earlier, William Lloyd Garrison began publishing his abolitionist newspaper _The Liberator_ here in 1831.
tossups.r: The memorial faces the gold-domed State House on Beacon Hill. For 10 points, name this capital of Massachusetts, the largest city in New England.

tossups.p: This city opened the first subway in the United States in 1897, under Tremont Street. Its Latin School, founded in 1635, is the oldest public school in the country, and its Common, set aside in 1634, is often called the oldest public park.
tossups.r: Its Puritan founders arrived with John Winthrop in 1630. For 10 points, name this New England city where the Freedom Trail begins.

tossups.p: _Publick Occurrences Both Forreign and Domestick_, often called the first newspaper printed in the American colonies, appeared in this city in 1690 but was shut down after one issue. Benjamin Franklin was born here in 1706 and wrote the Silence Dogood letters for his brother’s newspaper.
tossups.r: Franklin then ran away to Philadelphia. For 10 points, name this city where Paul Revere and Samuel Adams were also born.

tossups.p: Phillis Wheatley, who was enslaved by a merchant family in this city, became the first African American woman to publish a book of poems in 1773. Three years earlier, Crispus Attucks was one of five colonists killed when British soldiers fired into a crowd on this city’s King Street.
tossups.r: This city’s harbor was the scene of a Tea Party in 1773. For 10 points, name this Massachusetts city, where that 1770 massacre took place.

tossups.p: Frederick Law Olmsted designed this city’s Emerald Necklace, a chain of parks, and its Back Bay neighborhood was built on filled-in tidal marshland. A huge highway project nicknamed the “Big Dig” moved this city’s Central Artery into tunnels and was finished in 2007.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this city on the Charles River, home of Faneuil Hall and Fenway Park.

tossups.p: The USS _Constitution_, nicknamed “Old Ironsides,” is docked at the Charlestown Navy Yard in this city as the world’s oldest commissioned warship afloat. Also in Charlestown, a granite obelisk marks a 1775 battle that was fought mostly on Breed’s Hill.
tossups.r: That battle is called Bunker Hill. For 10 points, name this capital of Massachusetts, where Paul Revere’s ride began.

clues.t: Capital and largest city of Massachusetts, and the biggest city in New England
Founded in 1630 by Puritans of the Massachusetts Bay Colony, led by John Winthrop
Site of the Massacre (1770) and the Tea Party (1773) that helped spark the American Revolution
Paul Revere began his midnight ride here (1775) after two lanterns were hung in the Old North Church
The Freedom Trail, a 2.5-mile red-brick path, links 16 historic sites
Winthrop hoped the colony would be “a city upon a hill” (his sermon “A Model of Christian Charity”)
Parliament’s Port Act (1774), one of the Intolerable Acts, closed its harbor until the tea was paid for
The British left on March 17, 1776, after Washington put Henry Knox’s cannons on Dorchester Heights; celebrated as Evacuation Day
Faneuil Hall, the “Cradle of Liberty”; the Declaration of Independence was read from the Old State House balcony (July 1776)
The Battle of Bunker Hill (1775) was fought mostly on Breed’s Hill in Charlestown, which later became part of the city
American firsts: its Common (1634, oldest public park), Latin School (1635, oldest public school), and the first U.S. subway (1897)
The USS _Constitution_ (“Old Ironsides”), the oldest commissioned warship afloat, is docked at the Charlestown Navy Yard
Benjamin Franklin was born here (1706) and wrote the Silence Dogood letters before moving to Philadelphia
William Lloyd Garrison published the abolitionist newspaper _The Liberator_ here, starting in 1831
Named for a town in Lincolnshire, England, where the Puritan minister John Cotton had preached
Built on the Shawmut Peninsula, first called Trimountaine; William Blaxton invited the Puritans to settle there
1721 smallpox epidemic: Cotton Mather pushed inoculation after learning of it from Onesimus, an enslaved African man
First public demonstration of ether anesthesia (1846, the Ether Dome); Alexander Graham Bell’s first telephone call (1876)
1919 police strike: Governor Calvin Coolidge said there is “no right to strike against the public safety”
Great Molasses Flood (1919): a burst tank flooded the North End, killing 21 people
Saint-Gaudens’s memorial on the Common honors Robert Gould Shaw and his Black regiment, the 54th Massachusetts (the film _Glory_)
_Publick Occurrences_ (1690), often called the first colonial newspaper, was printed here and shut down after one issue
Phillis Wheatley, enslaved here, became the first African American woman to publish a book of poems (1773)
Crispus Attucks was among five colonists killed on King Street in 1770
Sexton Robert Newman hung the two lanterns (“two if by sea”) in the Old North Church steeple
Olmsted’s Emerald Necklace parks; the “Big Dig” moved the Central Artery highway into tunnels (finished 2007)

trap.title: City, colony, or event?
trap.body: Many Boston clues are really about events and places that have their own answer lines. If a question asks for “this event,” it may want the Boston Massacre or the Boston Tea Party; if it asks for “this colony” or “this state,” it wants Massachusetts. Saying “Massachusetts” when the question asks for “this city” is wrong, and so is naming the city when the question wants the event.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this city” or “this town” means Boston, “this event” means the Massacre or the Tea Party, and “this colony” or “this state” means Massachusetts. Don’t mix Boston up with Philadelphia (Independence Hall, the Liberty Bell) or with Cambridge, home of Harvard, just across the Charles River.

topics.name: Harriet Tubman
topics.kicker: Underground Railroad conductor · Union scout and spy in the Civil War
topics.briefing: Born into slavery in Maryland around 1822, Harriet Tubman escaped to Philadelphia in 1849, then went back again and again to lead family members and others to freedom on the Underground Railroad. People called her “Moses.” During the Civil War she worked as a Union scout, nurse, and spy, and she helped guide the Combahee River Raid, which freed more than 700 enslaved people in South Carolina.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In June 1863, this woman helped guide Colonel James Montgomery’s Black Union soldiers up the Combahee [“KUM-bee”] River in South Carolina, after her scouts found where Confederates had placed underwater mines. Union gunboats in that raid carried more than 700 enslaved people to freedom.
tossups.r: She had worked for the Union Army as a scout, nurse, and spy. For 10 points, name this Underground Railroad conductor nicknamed “Moses.”

tossups.p: As a teenager, this woman was badly hurt when an overseer threw a heavy metal weight that struck her head, and for the rest of her life she had sudden sleeping spells and vivid dreams she believed came from God. She was born with the first name Araminta on Maryland’s Eastern Shore.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman who escaped slavery in 1849 and then led others north on the Underground Railroad.

tossups.p: The Quaker stationmaster Thomas Garrett often sheltered this woman and the freedom seekers she guided in Wilmington, Delaware, and William Still recorded their arrivals in Philadelphia. After the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, this woman began leading groups all the way to St. Catharines in Canada.
tossups.r: She had escaped from slavery in Maryland in 1849. For 10 points, name this Underground Railroad conductor nicknamed “Moses.”

tossups.p: John Brown called this woman “General” and asked her to help recruit fighters for his 1859 raid on Harpers Ferry, though she did not take part in the attack. Brown met her in Canada, where she had settled after leading many freedom seekers there.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman who escaped slavery in Maryland and became a famous conductor on the Underground Railroad.

tossups.p: Senator William Seward sold this woman land in Auburn, New York, where she later opened a home for elderly African Americans. She was buried in Auburn with military honors in 1913, after spending decades asking the government for a pension for her own Civil War service.
tossups.r: Abolitionists called her “Moses.” For 10 points, name this woman who led enslaved people to freedom on the Underground Railroad.

tossups.p: This woman once boasted, “I never ran my train off the track and I never lost a passenger.” She made about thirteen trips back to Maryland and led about seventy people to freedom, including her parents and several of her brothers.
tossups.r: She had escaped from slavery herself in 1849. For 10 points, name this most famous conductor on the Underground Railroad.

tossups.p: Cynthia Erivo earned an Oscar nomination for playing this woman in a 2019 film. National historical parks honoring this woman were created in the 2010s on Maryland’s Eastern Shore, where she was born, and in Auburn, New York, where she died.
tossups.r: In 2016, the Treasury announced plans to put her on the front of the $20 bill, replacing Andrew Jackson. For 10 points, name this Underground Railroad conductor.

tossups.p: During the Civil War, this woman worked in Beaufort [“BYOO-fert”], South Carolina, where she nursed sick soldiers and freedpeople and led a network of scouts who gathered information behind Confederate lines. Because she was rarely paid, she supported herself by selling pies and root beer that she made.
tossups.r: In 1863, she helped lead a raid up the Combahee River. For 10 points, name this former Underground Railroad conductor.

tossups.p: This woman’s first husband, John, was a free Black man who stayed behind when she escaped, and when she returned for him in 1851, he had married another woman. After the Civil War, she married a younger Union veteran named Nelson Davis in Auburn, New York.
tossups.r: She had escaped slavery in Maryland in 1849. For 10 points, name this woman known as the “Moses” of her people.

tossups.p: In 1857, this woman rescued her elderly parents, Ben and Rit, from Maryland after her father came under suspicion for helping freedom seekers. Over the Christmas holiday in 1854, she had led three of her brothers to freedom.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman who escaped slavery in 1849 and became the Underground Railroad’s most famous conductor.

tossups.p: In 1860, this woman helped a crowd in Troy, New York, free Charles Nalle, a man who had escaped slavery and was about to be sent back south under the Fugitive Slave Act. She had led many freedom seekers through New York to Canada.
tossups.r: Earlier, she had escaped from Maryland. For 10 points, name this conductor on the Underground Railroad, who was known as “Moses.”

tossups.p: When her enslaver, Edward Brodess, died in 1849, this woman feared she would be sold away from her family. Around the time she married in 1844, she had begun using her mother’s first name instead of the name Araminta.
tossups.r: Soon after Brodess died, she escaped to Philadelphia. For 10 points, name this woman who became the most famous conductor on the Underground Railroad.

tossups.p: In an 1868 letter, Frederick Douglass told this woman that “the midnight sky and the silent stars” had been the witnesses of her devotion to freedom and her heroism. Douglass contrasted her secret, dangerous work at night with his own public work by day.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman who escaped slavery and became famous as a conductor on the Underground Railroad.

tossups.p: Sarah Bradford wrote two biographies of this woman, in 1869 and 1886, to raise money for her. In her later years, this woman traveled to Boston, New York, and Washington, D.C., to speak in favor of women’s right to vote.
tossups.r: Bradford’s second book called her “the Moses of her people.” For 10 points, name this Underground Railroad conductor.

tossups.p: Between rescue missions, this woman worked as a cook and maid in Philadelphia and in hotels in Cape May, New Jersey, to save money for her trips back to Maryland. She guided her groups mostly at night, often following the North Star.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman who led about seventy people out of slavery on the Underground Railroad.

clues.t: The most famous “conductor” on the Underground Railroad, guiding enslaved people north to freedom
Nicknamed “Moses” for leading her people out of slavery
Escaped from slavery in Maryland in 1849, reaching Philadelphia
Served the Union Army as a scout, nurse, and spy during the Civil War
In 2016, the Treasury announced plans to put her on the front of the $20 bill, replacing Andrew Jackson
Combahee River Raid (June 1863): helped guide Union soldiers who freed more than 700 enslaved people in South Carolina
Made about 13 trips and led about 70 people to freedom; said she “never lost a passenger”
Born with the name Araminta (“Minty”) around 1822 in Dorchester County, Maryland; later took her mother’s first name
John Brown called her “General” and sought her help recruiting for his raid on Harpers Ferry (1859)
Bought land in Auburn, New York, from William Seward; opened a home for elderly African Americans; died there in 1913
After the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, led freedom seekers all the way to St. Catharines, Canada
As a teen, a heavy weight thrown by an overseer struck her head, causing lifelong sleeping spells and visions
In her later years, spoke in favor of women’s suffrage in Boston, New York, and Washington, D.C.
Sheltered by Quaker stationmaster Thomas Garrett in Wilmington, Delaware; William Still recorded her arrivals in Philadelphia
Guided Colonel James Montgomery’s Black soldiers on the Combahee raid; her scouts found the Confederates’ river mines
Worked in Beaufort, South Carolina, nursing soldiers and leading scouts; sold pies and root beer to support herself
Escaped after her enslaver, Edward Brodess, died in 1849 and she feared being sold
Her first husband, John, a free Black man, had remarried when she came back for him (1851); she later married veteran Nelson Davis (1869)
Led three brothers to freedom at Christmas 1854; rescued her elderly parents, Ben and Rit, in 1857
Helped a crowd free Charles Nalle from federal custody in Troy, New York (1860)
Sarah Bradford’s biographies (1869, 1886) raised money for her; the second called her “the Moses of her people”
Frederick Douglass wrote that “the midnight sky and the silent stars” had witnessed her heroism (1868)
Played by Cynthia Erivo in a 2019 film; national historical parks honor her in Maryland and in Auburn, New York
Asked the government for decades for a pension for her own war service; buried with military honors
Worked as a cook and maid in Philadelphia and Cape May, New Jersey, to pay for her rescue trips

trap.title: Tubman, Truth, or Stowe?
trap.body: Three famous antislavery women get mixed up. Harriet Tubman escaped slavery and led others to freedom on the Underground Railroad. Sojourner Truth, born Isabella Baumfree in New York, was a speaker famous for her “Ain’t I a Woman?” speech. Harriet Beecher Stowe was a white author who wrote _Uncle Tom’s Cabin_. Players who hear “Harriet” and an antislavery clue sometimes blurt out the wrong one.
trap.fix: Tubman clues: born Araminta in Maryland, “Moses,” the Combahee River Raid, John Brown’s “General,” Auburn, New York, and the $20 bill plan. Truth clues: her speech in Akron, Ohio, and her New York childhood. Stowe clues: _Uncle Tom’s Cabin_ and Little Eva. Saying just “Tubman” is enough.
trap.line: Real answer line: Harriet Tubman (accept Araminta Ross)

topics.name: John Marshall
topics.kicker: Longest-serving Chief Justice · Established judicial review in 1803
topics.briefing: John Marshall spent a winter at Valley Forge, served as John Adams’s secretary of state, and then led the Supreme Court for more than 34 years, longer than any other Chief Justice. In _Marbury v. Madison_ (1803), his Court claimed the power of judicial review, the right to strike down laws that break the Constitution. Rulings like _McCulloch v. Maryland_ and _Gibbons v. Ogden_ made the national government, and the Court itself, far stronger.
topics.answerHtml: John Marshall (do not accept “Thurgood Marshall” or “George Marshall”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: According to legend, the Liberty Bell cracked while ringing for this man’s funeral in 1835. His death ended a record term of more than 34 years in his job, and Andrew Jackson chose Roger Taney [“TAW-nee”] to replace him.
tossups.r: He had been appointed by John Adams in 1801. For 10 points, name this Chief Justice who wrote the opinion in _Marbury v. Madison_.

tossups.p: This man, Charles Cotesworth Pinckney, and Elbridge Gerry were the three American diplomats who refused to pay a bribe to French agents in the XYZ Affair. He returned home a hero, won a seat in Congress, and became John Adams’s secretary of state.
tossups.r: Adams then appointed him Chief Justice. For 10 points, name this man who led the Supreme Court from 1801 to 1835.

tossups.p: In 1807, this judge presided over Aaron Burr’s treason trial in Richmond. Burr was found not guilty because this judge ruled that treason required proof, from two witnesses, of an actual act of war against the United States.
tossups.r: He also wrote the Court’s opinion in _McCulloch v. Maryland_. For 10 points, name this Chief Justice who established judicial review.

tossups.p: This judge wrote that “the power to tax involves the power to destroy” in a case that stopped Maryland from taxing the Second Bank of the United States. In that same 1819 opinion, he upheld Congress’s implied powers under the Necessary and Proper Clause.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Chief Justice who wrote both _McCulloch v. Maryland_ and _Marbury v. Madison_.

tossups.p: This judge’s opinion in _Fletcher v. Peck_ was one of the first times the Supreme Court struck down a state law, after Georgia’s legislature tried to cancel land sales tied to the Yazoo land scandal. He ruled that those sales were contracts Georgia could not break.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Chief Justice from 1801 to 1835, whose Court also decided _Marbury v. Madison_.

tossups.p: During the American Revolution, this future judge spent the winter at Valley Forge and fought at the battles of Brandywine, Germantown, and Monmouth. Later, he wrote a five-volume biography of his former commander, George Washington.
tossups.r: His opinion in _Marbury v. Madison_ established judicial review. For 10 points, name this Virginian who became the fourth Chief Justice of the United States.

tossups.p: This judge struck down a steamboat monopoly that New York had granted to Robert Fulton and Robert Livingston, ruling in _Gibbons v. Ogden_ that Congress has the power to regulate commerce between the states. Daniel Webster argued for the winning side in that 1824 case.
tossups.r: He served on the Court from 1801 until 1835. For 10 points, name this Chief Justice who also wrote _Marbury v. Madison_.

tossups.p: In _Cherokee Nation v. Georgia_, this judge called Native nations like the Cherokee “domestic dependent nations.” A year later, this judge ruled that Georgia’s laws had no force inside the Cherokee Nation, and Andrew Jackson supposedly replied that this man “has made his decision; now let him enforce it.”
tossups.r: That 1832 case was _Worcester v. Georgia_. For 10 points, name this Chief Justice, who also wrote _Marbury v. Madison_.

tossups.p: This judge declared that “it is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is.” In that same opinion, he struck down part of the Judiciary Act of 1789, the first time the Supreme Court overturned an act of Congress.
tossups.r: That 1803 case, _Marbury v. Madison_, established the power of judicial review. For 10 points, name this Chief Justice.

tossups.p: This man served briefly in the House of Representatives before becoming John Adams’s secretary of state. While still in that cabinet job in early 1801, he was confirmed to a new position, and he left several commissions for the “midnight judges” undelivered when Adams’s term ended.
tossups.r: One of those commissions belonged to William Marbury. For 10 points, name this man who became Chief Justice in 1801.

tossups.p: In one of his last major rulings, this judge held in _Barron v. Baltimore_ that the Bill of Rights limited only the national government, not the states. Earlier, in _Cohens v. Virginia_, he ruled that the Supreme Court could review state court decisions.
tossups.r: He was appointed by John Adams. For 10 points, name this Chief Justice who served from 1801 until his death in 1835.

tossups.p: This man briefly studied law under George Wythe [“WITH”] at the College of William & Mary, and he later argued for the Constitution at Virginia’s ratifying convention in 1788. Thomas Jefferson, his distant cousin, became one of his fiercest political enemies.
tossups.r: As Chief Justice, he wrote _Marbury v. Madison_. For 10 points, name this Federalist whom John Adams appointed Chief Justice in 1801.

tossups.p: This judge ended the practice of each justice writing a separate opinion and had the Supreme Court speak with one voice in an “opinion of the Court,” which he often wrote himself. He was appointed in the final weeks of John Adams’s presidency.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fourth Chief Justice of the United States, who wrote _Marbury v. Madison_.

tossups.p: Born in a log cabin on the Virginia frontier in 1755, this man was the oldest of fifteen children. He became a leading lawyer in Richmond, served in Virginia’s House of Delegates, and was elected to the U.S. House of Representatives in 1799.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Virginian who served as Chief Justice for more than 34 years.

tossups.p: During the case _Dartmouth College v. Woodward_, Daniel Webster told this judge’s Court, “It is, sir, as I have said, a small college. And yet there are those who love it!” This judge’s opinion ruled that the college’s charter was a contract that New Hampshire could not break.
tossups.r: That case was decided in 1819, the same year as _McCulloch v. Maryland_. For 10 points, name this Chief Justice, whose Court also decided _Marbury v. Madison_.

clues.t: 4th Chief Justice of the United States (1801–1835), the longest-serving Chief Justice
Wrote _Marbury v. Madison_ (1803), which established judicial review
Appointed by John Adams in 1801, near the end of Adams’s presidency
A Federalist from Virginia whose rulings made the national government and the Supreme Court stronger
_McCulloch v. Maryland_ (1819): states can’t tax the national bank; “the power to tax involves the power to destroy”
_Gibbons v. Ogden_ (1824): Congress regulates commerce between states; struck down New York’s steamboat monopoly
_Worcester v. Georgia_ (1832) sided with the Cherokee; Jackson supposedly said he “has made his decision; now let him enforce it”
One of the three U.S. diplomats in the XYZ Affair (1797–1798), with Charles Cotesworth Pinckney and Elbridge Gerry
John Adams’s secretary of state (1800–1801); left some “midnight judges” commissions undelivered, including Marbury’s
_Dartmouth College v. Woodward_ (1819): a college charter is a contract that a state can’t break
Presided over Aaron Burr’s treason trial (1807); Burr was found not guilty
Died in 1835; Andrew Jackson chose Roger Taney to replace him
Legend says the Liberty Bell cracked while ringing for his funeral (1835)
Wrote that “it is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is”
_Marbury_ struck down part of the Judiciary Act of 1789, the first time the Court overturned an act of Congress
_Fletcher v. Peck_ (1810): one of the first times the Court struck down a state law (Georgia’s Yazoo land scandal)
_Cherokee Nation v. Georgia_ (1831): called Native nations like the Cherokee “domestic dependent nations”
_Barron v. Baltimore_ (1833): the Bill of Rights limited only the federal government, not the states
_Cohens v. Virginia_ (1821): the Supreme Court can review state court decisions
Continental Army officer at Valley Forge; fought at Brandywine, Germantown, and Monmouth
Wrote a five-volume biography, _The Life of George Washington_
Replaced separate opinions by each justice with a single “opinion of the Court”
A distant cousin and bitter political rival of Thomas Jefferson
Studied law under George Wythe at William & Mary; backed the Constitution at Virginia’s ratifying convention (1788)
In the Dartmouth case, Daniel Webster argued, “It is... a small college. And yet there are those who love it!”
Born in a log cabin in Virginia (1755), the oldest of fifteen children

trap.title: Which Marshall?
trap.body: Several famous Marshalls show up in American history. John Marshall was the fourth Chief Justice (1801–1835). Thurgood Marshall argued _Brown v. Board of Education_ and became the first African American Supreme Court justice in 1967. George C. Marshall was the World War II general behind the Marshall Plan to rebuild Europe. And John Marshall Harlan, a different justice, wrote the lone dissent in _Plessy v. Ferguson_. Saying the wrong first name loses the tossup.
trap.fix: John Marshall clues: _Marbury v. Madison_ and judicial review, _McCulloch v. Maryland_, _Gibbons v. Ogden_, the XYZ Affair, Aaron Burr’s treason trial, and the Liberty Bell legend. _Brown v. Board_ or the NAACP means Thurgood; rebuilding postwar Europe means George. “Marshall” alone is fine, but say “John” if you have time.
trap.line: Real answer line: John Marshall (do not accept “Thurgood Marshall” or “George Marshall”)
